    #124237. Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1117 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights.
    • According to recent reports, before the court is a petition to review the U.S.
    • Sources indicate that though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock), Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “atmosphere” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

    According to recent reports, before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline tech giant. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

    Sources indicate that though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in Oneida County v. Oneida Indian Nation, which held that there is a federal common law cause of action allowing Indigenous property owners to bring trespass actions in federal court.

    In a recent development, the Andeavor case has been accompanied in recent years by a slate of lower court decisions similarly diminishing Indigenous property rights. In Davilla v. Enable Midstream Partners, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit held that a pipeline trespasser on Indigenous property would not be ordered to remove the pipeline until the federal district court decided it was, among other things, in the “public interest” to do so. Under federal law, federal courts may not order injunctive relief unless such relief is in the public interest. The 10th Circuit’s decision imposed a public interest standard on Indigenous property when, arguably, it would not have done so in relation to private property.

    It has been revealed that similarly, a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin held in Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe Indians v. Enbridge Inc. that the tribe was not entitled to the immediate removal of a trespassing pipeline because the public interest favored its continued operation. Fortunately, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit reversed that decision. Other federal courts have also ordered immediate eviction of trespassers to Indigenous lands (e.g., United States v. Osage Wind), but the judiciary tends to invoke the public interest when favoring pipeline or other petroleum industry companies.

    Newland argues that some judges may be channeling a long tradition where the federal government assumed that Indigenous property is public property: Most pipelines running through Indigenous lands now originated in an earlier era where the federal government assumed a kind of guardianship over tribal nations, where the Interior Department granted easements and rights-of-way over Indigenous lands without tribal consent. For example, the Supreme Court once held that the secretary of the Interior was empowered to concern leases to natural resources extraction companies even over tribal opposition (Cherokee Nation v. Hitchcock).

    The tradition of guardianship arose in early Supreme Court decisions comparing the federal-tribal relationship to a “guardian-ward” relationship (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia). Congress did not enact laws generally asserting actual guardianship over tribal nations; instead, the relationship was more accurately characterized as a trust relationship, with federal government owning and managing tribal and individual Indian asserts in trust.

    A trust beneficiary has legal rights that a ward does not. A ward does not possess the legal capacity to make their own decisions, while tribal nations and tribal citizens do. When federal or state actors did assert guardianship over Indigenous assets, tragedy often followed, as evidenced in the early 20th century killings of Osage people fictionalized in the film “Killers of the Flower Moon” or in the flooding of several Indian reservations in the mid-20th century by federal hydroelectric dam projects.

    Often, when tribal nations attempted to assert their own legal rights, the judiciary allowed the federal government to block those efforts. Justice Neil Gorsuch recently raised this matter in his dissent in Arizona v. Navajo Nation, where he pointed out that, decades ago, the federal government blocked the Navajo Nation from asserting their water rights, which remain unsettled to this day. In those older cases, the fact that the federal government could stand in the shoes of Indigenous interests suggested that Indigenous property was therefore, in effect, public property.

    Recent findings suggest that the Department of Justice’s litigation positions also frequently hearken back to expansive federal controls over Indigenous property. While the Supreme Court has explicitly overturned the earlier cases analogizing the federal-tribal relationship as a guardianship in cases such as United States v. Sioux Nation, DOJ attorneys are known to continue to assert guardianship-type control over Indigenous property. Indeed, federal judges have sanctioned them for making such claims post-Sioux Nation.

    In a recent development, this legacy of guardianship once again has raised its head. D.C. Circuit briefing has concluded in a claim brought by the Tohono O’Odham Nation against the Department of Homeland Security regarding the administration’s proposal to build a border wall on the tribe’s land. The tribe argues that the federal common law cause of action recognized in Oneida undergirds the suit. In response, the DOJ now asserts that tribal nations may not sue the United States for trespass on hands held in trust by the federal government for the benefit of a tribal nation. This claim rings again of guardianship, where a ward normally does not have the legal capacity to sue their guardian.

    The import of the government’s claim in the border wall case, like the trespass action in Andeavor, has enormous consequences for Indian country: If the government can confiscate Indigenous property held in trust by the United States, then the judiciary will have allowed the federal government to reassume a guardianship-type relationship regardless of tribal consent or the federal government’s trust duties.

    Matthew L.M. Fletcher is the Harry Burns Hutchins Collegiate Professor of Law at the University of Michigan Law School.

    Recommended Citation: Matthew L.M. Fletcher, Tribal property and the Supreme Court, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 13, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/tribal-property-and-the-supreme-court/.

    Sources indicate that democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate are increasing their scrutiny of nine major law firms’ agreements with the Trump administration last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services.     The firm also provided free legal services to the Postal Service and the ​International Development Finance Corporation, according to a story by Reuters.

    Kirkland & Ellis turned down requests to work on specific projects for the Trump administration, including the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and challenges to the Postal Service’s handling of mail ballots, according to a story by CBS News.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that cloudLinux is the maker of Imunify360 — a suite of security products protecting millions of websites across the web hosting industry — and of CloudLinux OS, the operating system behind a large share of the world's shared hosting. To learn more about our company and products, visit our websites: cloudlinux.com and imunify360.com. Alongside those established product lines we run a small innovation team whose job is to find and prove the next ones.

    We are looking for a Product Owner to lead that team: a small, senior, fully remote squad of engineers that takes latest product concepts from idea to a working MVP in customers' hands, then hands proven products to a product line and moves on to the next concept. You will be accountable for the pipeline of ideas, the speed and rigour with which they are tested, and the evidence behind every go / no-go recommendation.

    According to recent reports, this is a hands-on lead role, not pure people management: roughly 50% discovery and leadership (customer conversations, scoping, prioritisation, coaching, reporting to the CPO) and 50% building (prototypes, spikes, design and code review, demo stands). You will not be the team's only builder, but you must be able to build a credible prototype yourself and hold a technical opinion about every part of it.

    You don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. If you have taken a product from nothing to its first paying customers before — as a founder, an early engineer, or the lead of an incubation team — and you get deep into unfamiliar technical territory fast, we will teach you the market.

    Industry observers note that the innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

    Prototyping and technical direction.

    We evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. Expect to use agents to build prototypes, generate test corpora and draft customer-facing material.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices unveiled that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

    The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

    Recent findings suggest that mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

    The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be rapidly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

    Sources indicate that the challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

    U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

    Industry observers note that A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

    Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”.

    It has been revealed that the D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

    Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most vital and effective pieces of the President’s response.”.

    Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he stated, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”.

    Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”.

    And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent plans to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”.

    In a recent development, the challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a upcoming removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”.

    Industry observers note that the statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”.

    Sources indicate that the challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they noted, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

    The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

    According to recent reports, the court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services manufacturer violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

    The firm asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

    According to recent reports, the investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors said, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”.

    In a recent development, in a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the company’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”.

    The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Justice Pierce Butler, who served on the Supreme Court from 1923 to 1939, died on this day in 1939. Butler was the first Minnesotan appointed to the Supreme Court and the only dissenter in the infamous case of Buck v. Bell (though he did not write anything).

    Industry observers note that on Friday, the justices met in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. That afternoon, they unveiled that they had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, a dispute over whether a financial-services organization violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering. For more on these cases, see the On Site section below.

    Industry observers note that additional orders from Friday’s conference are expected this morning at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    The December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that new research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.
    • Latest research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.
    • According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that new research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images).

    Latest research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

    According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

    In a recent development, among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that indicated signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

    It has been revealed that researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They stated AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

    “The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

    #124198. Tech Report: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1327 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his newly introduced book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • In a recent development, in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his newly introduced book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he mentioned, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    In a recent development, in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    Industry observers note that for most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    Industry observers note that the court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    According to recent reports, but I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    Another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    Sources indicate that that leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    Alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    Recent findings suggest that as I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    The administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    Pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    The 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    The new term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    Alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the new term.

    Sources indicate that the 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    So Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the matter-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    Dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    #124194. Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1861 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • Sources indicate that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    Sources indicate that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    In a recent development, for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    According to recent reports, similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    In a recent development, one consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    According to recent reports, for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual customers of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    According to recent reports, if the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    It has been revealed that this criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Sources indicate that finally, and most important in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Industry observers note that sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    In a recent development, sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    Recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    Bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    According to recent reports, from an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Industry observers note that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky says, courts must decide: which tradition?

    The existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at issue in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    In a recent development, recommended Citation: Haley Proctor, Listening to the past, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/listening-to-the-past/.

    Tech Report: The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I rapidly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I rapidly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    According to recent reports, satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each latest matter at the outset?

    Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material issues in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or problem. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    It has been revealed that satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    Ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    It has been revealed that chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our latest law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Recent findings suggest that satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same plan from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati noted earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    It has been revealed that chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely crucial, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be noted in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

    Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce fresh technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

    #124188. Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    According to recent reports, the court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services firm violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    It has been revealed that the research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    According to recent reports, thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    Recent findings suggest that in June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    Recent findings suggest that in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    In their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Industry observers note that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    According to recent reports, khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    After the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they mentioned, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    The Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the issue at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    It has been revealed that on Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    In rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    Maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at issue in this case, the state said, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    It has been revealed that in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    Strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At matter in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    It has been revealed that and in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    In its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Fresh York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    It has been revealed that the United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    Justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.
