    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent newly introduced book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent newly introduced book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history highlights that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    It has been revealed that shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Industry observers note that shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    In a recent development, but this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    It has been revealed that chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    Recent findings suggest that marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    Recent findings suggest that nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political problems as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Newly introduced York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Recent findings suggest that yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Industry observers note that shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Latest York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    It has been revealed that justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    It has been revealed that again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to matter a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a upcoming story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    Sources indicate that if I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    In a recent development, regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    In a recent development, recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A postmortem examination revealed that a swallowed hat became lodged in Fiona the hippoâs digestive tract, leading to her death at the Cincinnati Zoo.

    CINCINNATI (AP) â A necropsy on Fiona the hippo demonstrated that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo noted Friday.

    In a recent development, fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old.

    The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement.

    It has been revealed that since her death, Fiona’s fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats. âShe brought so much love in her lifetime,â remarked one note.

    Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many â from teachers to parents to children.

    During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for âanyone that was going through hard times.â.

    Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years.

    âThe support that weâre feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," mentioned Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. “She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles.â.

    One of Fiona’s keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member.

    According to recent reports, âIt has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire,â Wingate wrote. âWe lost her in the most horrific and tragic way.â.

    Industry observers note that she ended: âShe was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry.â.

    Fiona wasnât the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object.

    In 1923, a hippo âcame to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth,â according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippoâs remains from the Cincinnati Zoo.

    Industry observers note that the Cincinnati Enquirer reported at the time that Zeekoe had a habit of opening his mouth wide to chomp cake and other treats tossed by guests. He died after swallowing a tennis ball, which zoo officials believed a child had dropped into the hippoâs mouth without realizing the harm it could cause.

    Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona’s digestive system wasn’t meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said.

    Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through.

    Industry observers note that blood work revealed her health was failing Thursday, so the zooâs animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, noted Mike Wenninger, the zooâs director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippoâs anatomy, he added.

    Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he noted.

    The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines.

    âNo treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked,â Wenninger remarked.

    Jenike called the zoo’s staff heroic in their efforts to save her.

    According to recent reports, at first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.

    But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials mentioned. By Monday, the zoo confirmed Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.

    The zoo’s animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.

    Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries.

    Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.

    Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure âthe smiles she gave me.â.

    Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.

    Recent findings suggest that the zoo’s staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn’t nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.

    In a recent development, she became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.

    Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

    By OBED LAMY and JOHN SEEWER Associated Press.

    Associated Press journalists Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Some sheriffs who cooperated with the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts lost their reelection bids as challengers pushed for changes in local law enforcement.
    • According to recent reports, GRAHAM, N.C.
    • The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County’s growing Latino community was so fractured, Long remarked, that the vehicle emblazoned with âsheriffâ made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some sheriffs who cooperated with the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts lost their reelection bids as challengers pushed for changes in local law enforcement.

    According to recent reports, GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) â As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administrationâs immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

    The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County’s growing Latino community was so fractured, Long remarked, that the vehicle emblazoned with âsheriffâ made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

    âTheyâve been living in fear. They feel like they donât have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they donât belong,â Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriffâs deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

    Sources indicate that johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trumpâs push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trumpâs crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration’s efforts.

    Industry observers note that johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under whatâs known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

    It has been revealed that the administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

    In a recent development, the AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate’s defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse â from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020.     Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure.     The county acquired the moniker âNo Chance Alamanceâ because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers mentioned.

    Voter Renee Russell said the sheriffâs cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the countyâs first Black sheriff, local media reported.

    But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson’s record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn’t think immigration played a significant role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

    It has been revealed that the sheriffâs office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

    Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

    âIn general, people are fed up with the sheriffâs negativeness about immigrants,â stated retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, who distributed emails, social media posts and campaign literature in support of Bickel.

    In Wisconsinâs Winnebago County, ICEâs arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.
    • According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both noted they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that newly introduced candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both noted they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that newly introduced candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith noted to Law.com.

    Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s notable to look at their options early.”.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • Sources indicate that but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • Before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    Sources indicate that but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile problems as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    Before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    According to recent reports, litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    Industry observers note that after a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    It has been revealed that once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court unveils in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    The court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    For a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely reveals that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    According to recent reports, once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile issues that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    In a recent development, one week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    This ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    Shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either presently serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    According to recent reports, in March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    Industry observers note that U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    On Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    Sources indicate that as expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    According to recent reports, this week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    Nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    According to recent reports, last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the concern will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    Sources indicate that in addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    In a recent development, in a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    Because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    As I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration challenges dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    Recent findings suggest that and there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    Suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    The responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    Industry observers note that the rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    Several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are currently considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, Latest Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the tech giant. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    Sources indicate that the responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    In its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to matter universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    After CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    Sources indicate that the case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    Sources indicate that that deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    The justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #124125. Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify.
    • Recent findings suggest that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton mentioned the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

    Recent findings suggest that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

    It has been revealed that it is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

    So how can one tell the difference?

    As we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

    Political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

    According to recent reports, the 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each new circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

    But circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

    According to recent reports, timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

    Sources indicate that to clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This demonstrates, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

    Finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

    In a recent development, the allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”.

    According to recent reports, jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    An Open Book: Law professor with bipolar disorder says people with mental illness can empower each other

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • #MyPathtoLaw celebrates the diversity of the legal profession through stories detailing attorneys’ unique and inspiring trajectories.
    • The most dangerous moments of Fredrick Vars’ life guided his career path.
    • The first came in fall 2004, when he was a third-year associate at a law firm then known as Miller Shakman & Beem in Chicago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    #MyPathtoLaw celebrates the diversity of the legal profession through stories detailing attorneys’ unique and inspiring trajectories.

    The most dangerous moments of Fredrick Vars’ life guided his career path.

    The first came in fall 2004, when he was a third-year associate at a law firm then known as Miller Shakman & Beem in Chicago.

    It has been revealed that just days after he’d won his first jury trial, representing a union member suing the union for retaliation, he experienced his first psychotic episode. Though he had dealt with depression much of his life, he’d later be diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

    It’s a day he barely remembers. His delusional behavior was so concerning that his wife called 911 for an ambulance.

    It has been revealed that “But who shows up? A police officer in uniform with a gun at the front door,” says Vars, the author of Through the Fire: How People with Mental Illness are Empowering Each Other. “I was so delusional. I don’t think I was nearly as afraid as I should have been in that situation.”.

    Vars, a Yale Law School graduate with a bachelor’s degree from Princeton University, recently had started a new medication.

    “That, combined with stress at work, was the trigger for the manic episode,” he indicates.

    He voluntarily committed himself to a Chicago psychiatric hospital, signing a paper that placed him in a locked psychiatric unit, a move that he’d later question.

    It has been revealed that “I really had no awareness of the law around mental health,” he indicates. “It just seemed crazy to me that my consent was given in a state where I had no idea what the paper I was signing said. How could that possibly be legal? That can’t be informed consent.”.

    After he was discharged and at home, he entered a deep depression, fighting suicidal ideation as he worked his way back.

    Recent findings suggest that “We lived in an apartment on the 12th floor, and I was afraid to go near the windows. I was afraid to go in the kitchen because there were knives. I just didn’t trust myself,” he indicates.

    He healed and went back to work, but in spring 2006, the second defining moment came. Facing stress and handling another medication change, he had another manic episode followed by another hospital stay.

    With the help of lithium, he stabilized and realized that he needed a career change.

    “It’s tough when your brain fails you,” he states.

    Inspired by his parents, both of whom had been professors at Oregon State University, he decided that he’d move into legal education.

    It has been revealed that he knew that he needed a job talk paper—a manuscript to be the foundation of his application—as he faced the academic interview process. He chose “the in-between status of voluntary hospitalization and commitment,” he states.

    Sources indicate that it worked. He was hired at the University of Alabama School of Law as an associate law professor in 2008. With help from medication and self-care, he claims, he received tenure.

    The biggest difference between practicing law and teaching, Vars says, is that now he can conduct research on the topic of his choice. He’s focused on firearms regulation and suicide prevention. Along with papers in academic journals, in 2020 Vars co-authored the book Weapon of Choice: Fighting Gun Violence While Respecting Gun Rights.

    Vars helped develop and has been an advocate for Donna’s Law, which establishes a voluntary self-registry creating a prohibition on firearm sales as a self-defense against suicide.“It’s a real passion project for me,” he states.

    Sources indicate that “Donna was a woman actually not too different from myself, dealing with bipolar disorder, had voluntarily admitted herself to psychiatric care multiple times,” Vars says. “After too many years of depression, she decided to impulsively purchase a gun and killed herself the same day.”.

    Suicide is the 10th leading cause of death in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

    Testifying about the self-registry before the Kansas legislature and in other states pushed Vars to become more open.

    Donna’s Law is now on the books in five states, but Vars’ goal is to have it enacted federally.

    “It would just take one bill to provide that option in 50 states,” he adds.

    For Vars, going public with his diagnosis has not been easy.

    Recent findings suggest that “I thought I’d tell the world, ‘Oh, I have bipolar disorder.’ But people generally are not listening. Disclosure is not a one-time thing. It’s an over-and-over process,” he indicates. “Each time, I have a little hesitancy, but it goes away more and more.”.

    While working on Donna’s Law, he started interviewing advocates, mostly people living with mental health challenges as well as their loved ones. Those conversations kick-started his work on Through the Fire.

    But in fall 2024, as he was finishing the book, he had to stop taking lithium, which was impacting his kidney function.

    After 18 years of stability, switching meds—combined with work pressure—sent him back to the hospital in a manic episode.

    In a recent development, “It was harder this time,” Vars notes. “I write about that in the epilogue.”.

    While he’s holding off on writing another book, he continues his teaching with seminars on mental health law.

    “A group of people who have really positively responded to my openness are my students. I make a point of saying, ‘If you ever need to talk to someone, we have counselors, they’re the professionals; but come knock on my door at any time,’” he says.

    Many do just that. Often, they are fearful of the questions on the character and fitness portion of the Alabama bar asking whether candidates have a condition, including mental health disorders, that might affect the ability to practice law.

    Some students say they are avoiding mental health treatment—fearful they’d receive a diagnosis and then have to respond yes to that question.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s a tricky one,” Vars notes. “The answer is almost certainly yes. You have to be forthcoming to the bar.”.

    Still, he advises that treatment is the biggest priority.

    “Get treatment early. Don’t let fear prevent you from getting treatment.” he notes. “Taking care of yourself is the best thing you can do. Can you still be a good lawyer? Yes, you can.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end people, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk.
    • think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end people, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the tech giant grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped promptly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

    think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

    take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

    translate security concerns into engineering action.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

    are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

    Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

    Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

    Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

    Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

    Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

    Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

    5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

    Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

    An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

    The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

    Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

    A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

    Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

    Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

    Incident response or application security experience.

    Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    In a recent development, liveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.
